<explanation>
This project is a full-stack resume builder application called Reactive Resume. Its purpose is to enable users to create, customize, share, and manage their resumes through a highly interactive and multi-lingual interface. The codebase is split into multiple apps and libraries, hinting at a modular architecture. Here’s how you can accurately represent its system design when drawing your diagram:

1. Main Components:
   • Frontend Applications:
     - “apps/client”: The main React (Vite) frontend that users interact with. It handles login, registration, resume building (with pages for authentication, builder, dashboard, home, etc.), and integrates detailed components such as various resume sections, theming, notifications, and localization.
     - “apps/artboard”: Likely a specialized part of the application for designing or previewing resume templates in real time. It includes its own set of components (templates, pages, etc.).
   • Backend Server:
     - “apps/server”: A NestJS-based backend that exposes APIs for authentication, resume management, user management, email services, storage, and more. Within this, modules are clearly separated (auth, contributors, feature, health, mail, printer, resume, storage, translation, user) which points to a micro-modular architectural style.
   • Shared Libraries:
     - “libs/dto”: Contains Data Transfer Objects used for standardizing communication between frontend and backend.
     - “libs/hooks”: Provides reusable React hooks for frontend logic.
     - “libs/parser” and “libs/schema”: Handle parsing of resume data, templates and schema validation.
     - “libs/ui”: Contains shared UI components used across different frontend parts.
     - “libs/utils”: Offers utility functions (such as array, string, date, and other namespace functions) used throughout the project.
   • Infrastructure and Tools:
     - Database and ORM: Uses PostgreSQL as the primary database along with Prisma ORM for database operations.
     - Object Storage: Minio is used for storing objects such as avatars, PDFs, and resume previews.
     - External Services: 
         ▪ OpenAI integration for functionalities like content improvement and tone adjustment.
         ▪ Browserless service for headless Chrome operations (PDF printing and preview generation).
         ▪ SMTP server for sending password recovery and other emails.
         ▪ OAuth providers (GitHub, Google) to allow for third-party authentication.
         ▪ Localization and translation through LinguiJS and Crowdin.
     - Containerization and Deployment Tools: Docker-related files and multiple Docker Compose files indicate containerized deployment and various environments (development, swarm, traefik-based setups).

2. Relationships and Data Flow:
   • The Frontend (both apps/client and apps/artboard) will interact with the backend server through RESTful APIs secured with JWT or other guards (note the existence of multiple authentication guards and strategies).
   • The backend server communicates with the database (Postgres) via Prisma ORM, manages file storage via Minio, and performs PDF generation via Browserless.
   • The shared libraries (DTOs, UI components, hooks, parser, utilities) ensure that both the frontend and backend adhere to a consistent contract and code reuse—thus, they fall into a “common” layer.
   • External integrations (SMTP, OAuth, OpenAI) are connected to the server module, and should be noted as external services with directional arrows showing API calls or data exchange.

3. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular Design: Different “apps” for client, artboard, and server along with logically segmented modules (auth, resume, storage, etc.) depict separation of concerns.
   • Micro-modular / Layered Architecture: Layers for UI, business logic, data access, and utilities are clearly differentiated.
   • API-First Communication: Consistent data contracts (provided by DTOs) are used between the frontend and backend.
   • Scalability & Extensibility: The libraries and consistent use of external configuration files (like Dockerfiles, Compose files) allow easy scaling, customization, and deployment.

4. Guidelines for Creating the Diagram:
   • Create clear blocks representing each main component. Lay out separate sections for client (React apps “client” and “artboard”), server (NestJS modules), database (Postgres), storage (Minio), and external services (OpenAI, Browserless, SMTP, OAuth providers, localization services).
   • Draw directional arrows:
         ▪ From frontend components to backend APIs (show login, resume updates, etc.)
         ▪ From backend to database and storage.
         ▪ From backend to external services.
         ▪ Emphasize data flow for authentication, resume creation, PDF generation, and translations.
   • Use distinct shapes or color coding to differentiate between:
         ▪ UI/Frontend components (e.g., rounded rectangles, one color).
         ▪ Backend modules or services (e.g., square blocks in another color).
         ▪ External services and infrastructure components (e.g., cloud icons or different shapes).
   • Label each component with its purpose. For example, “Auth Module (NestJS)” or “Resume Builder (React)”.
   • Include notes on design patterns, like “shared DTOs for data consistency” and “modular architecture with separate libraries” wherever relevant.

5. Tailoring the Diagram to Reactive Resume:
   • Emphasize the separation between the two frontends (client for general user interaction and artboard for template design/preview) and the NestJS backend.
   • Highlight the integration points: PostgreSQL for data persistence; Minio for storing media; Browserless for PDF generation; external services for authentication (GitHub, Google) and OpenAI features.
   • Make sure to call out that the system uses modern technologies (React, Vite, NestJS, Prisma) and includes robust localization support managed by external tools.
   • Indicate configuration/deployment tools on the periphery if needed (Dockerfile, Docker Compose, etc.) to show how the system is containerized and ready for easy self-hosting.

When drawing your diagram, strive for clarity and detail—every box should be clearly labeled and every connection line should represent a clear dependency or data flow. This detailed breakdown will help capture the essential elements of Reactive Resume’s architecture and provide a comprehensive overview tailored for any principal software engineer reviewing the system design.
</explanation>
